articles.title: Something is wrong: triage a suspected security incident
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Start here when the cause is unclear: establish impact, protect people, preserve facts and choose a response path.

body.p: Use when someone reports suspicious activity, missing information or an unexplained outage. An alert is a lead, not proof of compromise.
Which service, account or device? What changed, when and in which time zone? Is harm continuing? Are safety, payments, personal data or administrator access involved?

1. Assign an incident lead and a recorder; use a trusted communication channel.
2. Stop the specific harmful activity using the narrowest reversible control available to an authorized responder.
3. Escalate safety risks to the responsible emergency or operations team before changing equipment.
Record observations separately from assumptions: timestamps, affected assets, alert IDs, actions, owners and outcomes. Preserve original logs in restricted storage.
Choose the closest playbook; combine account, endpoint and data-loss paths when needed. Agree service priorities, a rollback plan and an owner before disruptive changes.
Require evidence that the entry point is addressed, essential work succeeds and monitoring works. Record unresolved uncertainty and who accepts residual risk.
Escalate uncontrolled spread, privileged compromise or unavailable evidence to an incident response specialist. Set the next update time and track follow-up fixes.

Create a working incident record: incident lead, affected service, first observation, current impact, next action, action owner and next update time. Mark each assertion as observed, inferred or unknown. For every proposed change, record expected benefit, possible interruption and how to reverse it. If the person responding lacks authority or cannot judge the operational impact, hand that change to the service owner; continue gathering safe facts. An unknown cause should not delay containing verified ongoing harm, but it should prevent claims that the problem is solved.
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: incident response — https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final

articles.title: I clicked a suspicious link: phishing and malicious messages
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Distinguish a message received, a link opened, credentials entered and software executed; each needs a different response.

body.p: Use for suspicious email, SMS, QR codes, collaboration messages or fake login pages. Receiving a message alone does not confirm compromise.
Did you only open a link, enter a password or one-time code, approve sign-in, download or run a file, or send money?

1. Stop interacting; do not reopen the link to investigate.
2. Report through your organization's trusted IT channel and retain the original message.
3. If credentials or approval were shared, use the account-takeover playbook from a known-clean device. If software ran, use the malware playbook.
Save the message with headers, message ID, approximate interaction time and affected account. Share suspicious URLs as text; never paste passwords or live tokens.
IT should review sign-in and endpoint alerts, then remove confirmed malicious messages using the mail platform. For a link-only visit, assess downloads and browser alerts before assuming infection.
Check affected accounts for unrecognized activity; confirm endpoint scans and mail controls complete. Tell the reporter the outcome without blame.
Use phishing-resistant authentication and an easy reporting route. Escalate money loss to finance immediately; contact the bank through verified details.

Branch on what the person actually did. Message received only: report and let IT assess distribution. Link opened only: check for downloads or alerts and watch account activity. Password entered or MFA approved: treat identity access as exposed. File executed or security protection disabled: escalate endpoint containment. Payment or bank details shared: engage finance separately. Record the answers in the case so the next responder does not need the person to repeat the event. Do not upload a confidential attachment to a public malware-analysis service to find out whether it is malicious.
Phishing: actions to take — https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/respond-recover/phishing

articles.title: A payment request looks wrong: business email compromise
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Stop a fraudulent payment, verify the request outside email and investigate the mailbox without losing transaction evidence.

body.p: Use for changed bank details, urgent transfers, gift-card requests or a trusted supplier thread that suddenly asks for unusual payment.
Was money sent? Which transaction and bank? Was the request verified through a previously known number? Could either mailbox be compromised?

1. Ask finance to pause the disputed payment and related changes.
2. If funds moved, contact your bank immediately using verified contact details and request its fraud/recovery process.
3. Verify the request by a separate trusted channel, not the number or reply address in the message.
Preserve original messages, headers, invoices, payment references, beneficiary details and callback notes in restricted incident records.
If mailbox access is suspected, follow account containment and review forwarding, mailbox rules and unauthorized delegates. Check whether other pending invoices were altered before resuming payments.
Finance independently confirms legitimate payment details. IT documents the mailbox findings and session cleanup. A recovery request is not proof funds were returned.
Require independent verification for bank-detail changes and dual approval for risky payments. Escalate actual loss to leadership and appropriate local law enforcement.

Keep finance and IT tasks separate but synchronized. Finance owns payment holds, bank communications and the record of attempted recovery. IT owns mailbox and identity investigation. Preserve an original copy of the suspicious invoice and compare it with a previously verified payment instruction; do not ask the potentially compromised thread to validate itself. Record who approved any resumed payment and the independent verification used. Inform counterparties through established contacts if their ongoing transactions may be affected, using the incident lead's approved communication plan.

articles.title: Files are encrypted: ransomware and extortion response
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Contain spread, protect backups and restore essential services only after the compromise path is addressed.

body.p: Use for ransom notes, unexplained mass encryption, deleted backups or an extortion claim. Treat possible data theft as a separate investigation.
Which systems are affected? Is encryption continuing? Are backups and identity systems reachable from compromised accounts? Which services affect safety?

1. Notify the incident lead using a trusted separate channel.
2. Authorized IT should isolate affected devices or network segments promptly while preserving management access where safe.
3. Protect backup administration. Do not connect backup media to an infected system or run an unverified decryptor.
Retain ransom notes, alert timelines, logs and affected-file examples. A qualified responder should decide forensic imaging and volatile-memory capture.

Keep isolated systems powered when safe; if isolation is impossible and spread continues, the incident lead must weigh shutdown against lost volatile evidence. Rebuild from trusted images, close entry points and reset affected credentials before staged restoration.
Test restored data and critical workflows in an isolated environment. Check for persistence and renewed encryption; the incident lead approves reconnection.
Escalate to specialist responders, insurer contacts where applicable and appropriate authorities. Payment decisions require leadership and legal advice; payment cannot guarantee recovery.

Separate containment from recovery decisions. A business owner should name the minimum service needed to continue essential work and the dependencies it requires. A responder should document why the selected restore environment and credentials are trusted. If evidence indicates stolen data, keep the breach investigation open even after files are restored. Do not use a demand note as proof of either data theft or successful decryption. Record any specialist advice and decision owner before a change that affects an entire site, identity system or backup estate.

#StopRansomware Guide — https://www.cisa.gov/stopransomware/ransomware-guide
Mitigating malware and ransomware attacks — https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/mitigating-malware-and-ransomware-attacks

articles.title: A computer may be infected: endpoint malware
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Isolate a suspect endpoint, preserve evidence and decide whether controlled cleanup or rebuilding is justified.

body.p: Use for antivirus or endpoint-detection alerts, unexpected processes, browser changes or unexplained connections. A slow computer alone is insufficient evidence.
What was detected and did it execute? Which user was signed in? Was privileged access available? Are other devices showing the same behavior?

1. Stop using the device for passwords or administrative work.
2. Ask authorized IT to isolate it through endpoint tooling or disconnect networking when safe.
3. Keep the alert and notify the device owner; do not delete files or reset the device before evidence decisions.
Record hostname, user, detection time, file hash, process lineage and connections from existing tools. Restrict access to exported logs or samples.

Use updated trusted security tools under IT direction. Investigate the initial entry point and related accounts. Where system integrity cannot be established, plan a clean rebuild after preserving evidence and needed data.
Confirm protections are active, persistence checks are complete and restored applications work. One clean scan does not prove all compromise is removed.
Patch the entry point and reduce unnecessary local administrator rights. Escalate credential theft, repeated detection or multiple affected devices.

Decide the next step from evidence and device function. A quarantined attachment that never executed may need scoped investigation; detected execution with credential access needs identity investigation as well. A shared server or medical/industrial device needs its owner involved before disconnection. Keep a record of what each remediation tool changed. If nobody can establish whether privileged persistence remains, record that uncertainty and plan specialist review or controlled rebuilding instead of repeatedly running the same scan.

articles.title: My account was taken over: passwords, MFA and session theft
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Recover trusted control, revoke sessions and inspect persistence; a password reset alone may leave access behind.

body.p: Use for unrecognized successful logins, unexpected MFA approvals, changed recovery details or messages sent without the account owner's knowledge.
Can the owner still sign in? Is the account privileged? Were sessions, recovery methods, OAuth grants, delegates or forwarding rules changed?

1. Use a known-clean device and the provider's official recovery route.
2. An authorized administrator should block risky access, revoke active sessions and reset compromised credentials.
3. Review authentication methods and remove unauthorized registrations after documenting them.
Export sign-in and audit events, authentication changes, mailbox rules and consent grants; preserve timestamps and identifiers without recording live tokens.

Review forwarding, delegates and application access; remove confirmed unauthorized persistence. Change reused passwords on other services. Re-enroll strong authentication after verifying the owner's identity.
Test legitimate sign-in and recovery routes. Confirm session revocation completed, recognizing provider delays; monitor for new sign-ins and repeated changes.
Prefer phishing-resistant MFA, separate administrator identities and monitored recovery procedures. Escalate administrator compromise or repeated access after reset to specialist responders.

Make an explicit inventory of access paths: password, active browser sessions, mobile applications, app passwords, recovery addresses, MFA methods and granted applications. Provider controls do not necessarily revoke all of these with one button. If the compromised account is the only administrator, use the provider's documented recovery or emergency-access procedure and avoid locking out the last trusted administrator without a recovery route. A user-visible successful login proves access was restored; it does not prove the attacker lost every other route.

articles.title: An API key was exposed: leaked cloud or application secrets
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Revoke the exposed credential and trace its use; deleting it from a repository does not make it safe again.

body.p: Use when a secret appears in source control, chat, logs, a public build artifact or an exposure alert.
Which credential and owner? What permissions, environments and workloads depend on it? When was it exposed? Could it mint temporary credentials?

1. Notify the credential owner and incident lead; do not paste the secret into tickets or chat.
2. Revoke or disable the exposed credential promptly. If continuity matters, coordinate a minimal replacement and verify the dependency switch.
3. Review and revoke derived sessions using provider-specific procedures.
Record credential identifier, exposure location and time range. Preserve audit logs, permission changes and affected workload identifiers in restricted storage.

Investigate new identities, policy changes, data access and unexpected resources. Update secret stores and dependent workloads; remove exposed copies after evidence capture. Repository history cleanup cannot invalidate a key.
Confirm the old credential is rejected through an authorized provider check; confirm replacement workloads work and suspicious activity stops. Review all relevant regions/accounts.
Use short-lived workload identities, least privilege and secret scanning. Escalate root, administrator, signing-key or multi-environment exposure immediately.

Treat the secret's permissions as the initial boundary of the investigation, then expand if logs show new credentials or privileges. Inventory services that will fail when the key is revoked and identify the owner responsible for each replacement. Do not grant a broader replacement role merely to make an error disappear. A provider-generated public identifier is not always a secret; confirm the credential type before rotating unrelated resources. Record the revocation timestamp and the earliest and latest suspicious events so downstream responders can correlate them.

Practical steps to minimize key exposure using AWS Security Services — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/practical-steps-to-minimize-key-exposure-using-aws-security-services/

articles.title: A critical vulnerability affects us: prioritize and remediate
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Confirm the affected asset and exposure, mitigate safely, and distinguish patch completion from incident recovery.

body.p: Use for a vendor alert, a relevant CISA KEV entry or credible exploitation evidence. A published CVE does not prove your asset is affected.
Which exact product/version/configuration? Is the vulnerable function reachable? Is it business-critical? Is there evidence of attempted or successful exploitation?

1. Match the vendor advisory to your inventory and assign an asset owner.
2. Prioritize exploitable internet-facing and high-impact assets; use KEV as evidence of known exploitation, not proof of a local breach.
3. Apply the vendor's temporary mitigation when a safe patch cannot be installed immediately.
Save affected versions, exposure checks, advisory URL, relevant logs and change records. Preserve compromise evidence before rebuilding.
Test the supported fix with a rollback plan, then deploy through an expedited change process. If compromise is suspected, investigate persistence and credential theft; patching alone is insufficient.
Recheck installed versions and configuration, perform an authorized non-destructive validation and test service health. Track exceptions with an owner and expiry.

Keep asset inventories and update ownership current. Escalate active exploitation or unsupported products. KEV deadlines for government bodies do not automatically define your organization's legal obligations.

Record one remediation row per affected deployment: asset, owner, version, reachable interface, evidence of exposure, mitigation, change time and validation result. Do not mark all installations fixed after updating a single server or container image. If a mitigation is temporary, schedule its replacement with the supported fix and retain its expiry owner. If an asset cannot be patched, the accountable owner must choose isolation, replacement or documented risk acceptance; the analyst should not silently close the finding because the patch failed.

articles.title: Our website may be breached: web application and API compromise
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Contain the affected route, preserve application evidence and fix the underlying authorization or input-handling defect.

body.p: Use for unauthorized records, changed site content, unexpected admin accounts or suspicious application execution.
Which route, tenant and account? Were data read or changed? Is the cause authorization, injection, vulnerable software or stolen credentials?

1. Involve the application owner and incident lead.
2. Apply a reversible restriction to the affected function; coordinate maintenance mode if narrow containment is insufficient.
3. Preserve relevant application, proxy and database audit logs before deployment changes.
Capture request IDs, time range, affected object IDs, actor IDs, deployment versions and changed files. Redact credentials and unnecessary personal data from shared copies.

Rebuild compromised runtime instances from trusted artifacts when needed. Correct authorization on every protected action; use parameterized database queries for injection flaws. Rotate secrets that the compromised runtime could access. Treat firewall rules as temporary mitigation.
Add a regression check using synthetic data: unauthorized users must fail and legitimate workflows must pass. Confirm affected deployments and background workers all receive the fix.
Keep audit logs protected and attributable. Escalate suspected data access to the breach process and suspected build compromise to the supply-chain playbook.

Use an explicit access test matrix with two test identities and synthetic records where possible: permitted user on its own record, unrelated user on that record and unauthenticated request. Validate both read and write paths relevant to the flaw. Keep active probing within the authorized environment and do not replay harmful requests against production data. If a runtime can access multiple tenants or databases, scope the investigation to those permissions rather than only the first reported record. Distinguish a blocked attempt from confirmed unauthorized access.

articles.title: Sensitive data may have left: exfiltration and data breach
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Stop ongoing exposure, establish what actually happened and support a qualified notification decision with evidence.

body.p: Use for unexpected bulk downloads, public sensitive files, suspicious exports or credible reports of stolen data.
What data and whose records? Was it accessed, merely exposed, altered or deleted? What time window and jurisdictions may be involved?

1. Notify the incident lead, data owner and privacy/legal contact immediately.
2. Restrict the specific account, share or transfer path causing ongoing exposure while preserving evidence.
3. Keep sensitive samples out of public tools and broad incident chats.
Preserve access/export logs, affected object lists, sharing changes and a timeline. Record logging gaps; absence of logs is not proof that access did not occur.
Close the exposure path, review related access and credentials, and validate the corrective change. Distinguish confirmed affected records from uncertain scope.
Test that unauthorized access fails and necessary access still works. Independently review the scope assessment, containment evidence and remaining unknowns.

Reduce unnecessary data access and retention. Legal/privacy owners determine applicable notification requirements and timing; do not wait for perfect certainty to involve them. Only authorized communications owners issue external statements.

Maintain two scope lists: confirmed affected data and potentially affected data that still needs investigation. For each, note supporting evidence, gaps and the next evidence source to request. Do not treat a screenshot or threat actor claim as a complete record count. The privacy/legal owner should receive updated facts as they develop, including when the organization first became aware. Technical containment can be complete while notification and customer-protection work remains open. This playbook supplies operational facts, not a jurisdiction-specific legal deadline.

articles.title: Our service is overwhelmed: suspected DDoS
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Separate traffic attacks from ordinary outages, engage the provider and verify legitimate customers can still use the service.

body.p: Use when service latency or errors rise with unusual request or network volume. Capacity faults and legitimate demand can look similar.
Is the bottleneck bandwidth, edge, origin or a specific expensive route? Is traffic reaching the origin directly? Which customer workflows are failing?

1. Contact the hosting/network/CDN incident channel with the affected service and start time.
2. Compare traffic, error and saturation metrics against normal behavior.
3. Apply targeted provider-supported mitigation with a rollback owner; preserve access for legitimate clients.
Keep traffic trends, targeted routes, request samples, provider event IDs and exact mitigation changes. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal data.

Tune rate limits and protection rules; restrict direct origin access where the architecture supports it. Use caching only where responses are safe to share. Broad challenges can break APIs and accessibility; test before widening them.
Measure successful customer transactions, latency and origin load from multiple locations. Falling traffic alone is not success if legitimate users are blocked.
Rehearse provider escalation and maintain capacity baselines. Escalate bandwidth saturation upstream; keep watching for unrelated account or data-access anomalies.

Start with a narrow rule and a known legitimate test workflow. Assign someone to monitor false positives while another responder checks whether the origin bottleneck improves. Capture the pre-change configuration and an expiry for emergency rules. Do not disable authentication, encryption or other security controls to recover throughput. If a traffic spike is legitimate demand, route it to capacity management instead of labeling users as attackers. If provider support recommends DNS or routing changes, assess propagation and rollback with the service owner.

articles.title: A work device is missing: lost or stolen laptop or phone
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Protect accounts and data using verified management tools, while avoiding irreversible erasure before an authorized decision.

body.p: Use when a work device or a personal device with work access is lost or stolen.
Was it unlocked? Is disk encryption confirmed? What accounts and local data were present? Is it managed, reachable or used for MFA?

1. Report the loss promptly to IT and physical security; record last known location and time.
2. Use the official device-management or lost-device service to lock it if available.
3. Revoke work sessions and suspend device access through authorized IT procedures.
Record asset ID, encryption/lock status, last check-in, management actions and account activity. A queued remote command is not proof it executed.

Replace access and authentication methods securely. Assess possible data exposure. Remote erasure requires an authorized decision considering data loss, evidence, ownership and recovery; do not remove tracking or activation protection casually.
Confirm lock or wipe status from management evidence, and verify the missing device can no longer access work services. Test the owner's replacement access.
Enable encryption, managed updates and screen locking. Escalate an unlocked privileged device or sensitive local data to the breach lead. Do not confront a suspected thief.

Separate device possession from account access. A locked device can still have valid service sessions, while revoking sessions cannot remove information already stored locally. Verify encryption using prior management records instead of assuming every company device had it enabled. If the device held recovery codes, administrator keys or access to backup administration, investigate those access paths explicitly. For personally owned devices, follow the organization's work-data management policy; a full-device erase can destroy unrelated personal information and should never be an automatic default.

Recovering a hacked account — https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/recovering-a-hacked-account

articles.title: An insider may be misusing access: investigate fairly
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Protect affected assets and assess observed behavior without treating a technical alert as proof of malicious intent.

body.p: Use for unexplained exports, unauthorized privilege changes or access inconsistent with an approved task. Mistakes and compromised accounts can resemble deliberate misuse.
What verified action occurred? Was it authorized? Which assets are exposed? Could automation, approved work or an external account takeover explain it?

1. Involve a small authorized team spanning security, HR and legal as appropriate.
2. Record facts and preserve relevant audit evidence; avoid accusations.
3. Limit access proportionately where there is an immediate risk, with an accountable owner.
Retain access, export and privilege-change records within approved retention and privacy boundaries. Keep the case restricted and document who handled evidence.
Compare activity with approved business needs. Coordinate access changes, offboarding or remedial training through established processes; do not improvise covert monitoring or employee searches.
Confirm risky permissions and sharing are corrected, necessary work continues, and the evidence supports each conclusion. Record alternate explanations and unresolved gaps.
Review privileged access regularly, separate sensitive duties and make reporting safe. Escalate threats to personal safety to the responsible safety team and appropriate authorities.

Write a neutral observation such as 'account exported a dataset outside its assigned task' and attach the evidence. Avoid labels such as 'malicious employee' until an authorized investigation supports them. Access logs identify credentials and actions, not necessarily the human who performed them. Coordinate any urgent access restriction with the case lead so evidence is preserved and essential services remain owned. Close the case with both technical findings and process corrections; do not use the playbook as an automated disciplinary decision.

articles.title: A supplier or software update is compromised
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Identify affected versions and access paths, pause unsafe distribution and verify replacement artifacts before restoring trust.

body.p: Use for a credible supplier breach notice, malicious dependency, altered build artifact or unauthorized activity through a vendor account.
Which exact version, package or integration? Was it deployed or only downloaded? What privileges and secrets did it have? Is the advisory authentic?

1. Verify the notice through a previously trusted vendor channel.
2. Inventory affected deployments and assign service owners.
3. Pause affected rollouts or integration access using the smallest safe reversible change.
Preserve package versions, hashes, lockfiles, build logs, artifact provenance, vendor messages and integration audit events.

Follow verified vendor guidance and independently check local exposure. For a compromised build path, restore trusted build inputs and rotate exposed credentials before rebuilding. A signed artifact can still be malicious if the signing path was compromised.
Confirm replacement provenance and deployed versions, review persistence and test business workflows. A supplier's statement of recovery does not establish your own systems are clean.
Maintain dependency inventories, scoped vendor access and release review. Escalate signing-key, build-system or widely deployed agent compromise to specialist responders.

Create a deployment map linking the affected component to each application, environment and owner. An unused package in a repository, an installed package and a package executed during a privileged build have different consequences. Ask the vendor for affected-version boundaries and recommended detection evidence, but retain your own timeline and audit records. Before reconnecting a supplier integration, confirm the replacement credentials have only the needed access and the supplier can describe the corrective action relevant to your exposure.

articles.title: Restore safely: backups and recovery after an incident
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Select a defensible restore point, validate it in isolation and reconnect only when both security and business checks pass.

body.p: Use after containment when essential systems or data need restoration. A backup-success notification is not evidence of a usable restore.
What service comes first? What dependencies and data-loss tolerance apply? Are backup credentials trusted? Which restore point predates the suspected compromise?

1. Agree restoration order with business owners.
2. Protect backup copies and administration from compromised identities.
3. Preserve needed evidence and choose a separate isolated recovery environment before restoring.
Record restore-point timestamps, backup integrity checks, selected images, dependencies, approvals and any known gap between backup time and compromise time.

Restore into clean, patched systems using trusted credentials. Scan and inspect recovered content; validate configuration and persistence risks. Do not overwrite the only surviving evidence or reconnect simply because files open.
Run an application-level restore test with the service owner: data integrity, key transactions, access controls and monitoring. Measure actual recovery time and data loss against agreed needs.
Test restores regularly, protect backup deletion and maintain independent recovery credentials. Escalate uncertain backup integrity or unavailable recovery keys before taking destructive steps.

Define pass/fail checks before restoring: which representative records must exist, which transaction must complete, which identity may access it and where alerts will appear. Record any data loss explicitly instead of calling a partial restore complete. If the selected restore point may contain the original compromise, hold reconnection until a qualified reviewer decides how to validate or replace it. Keep the old recovery copy available until the new service and a fresh protected backup have both been verified.

Ransomware-resistant backups — https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/ransomware-resistant-backups
Mitigating malware and ransomware attacks — https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/mitigating-malware-and-ransomware-attacks

articles.title: Cloud files are public: exposed storage and sharing
articles.author: Sentinel editorial synthesis (AI-assisted)
articles.snippet: Remove unintended public access, preserve the exposure timeline and validate both anonymous denial and intended access.

body.p: Use for public buckets, unintended document links, broad external shares or a scanner reporting sensitive objects accessible anonymously.
Was public access intended? Which objects, policies and links are affected? How long? Are logs available? Could authenticated outsiders also access them?

1. Confirm the specific exposure using authorized checks without downloading unnecessary sensitive data.
2. Notify the data and service owners.
3. Restrict unintended sharing or public policy; account for legitimate public-site dependencies before broad changes.
Record object identifiers, sharing configuration, policy-change times and available access logs. Preserve a restricted configuration snapshot before changes.

For S3, inspect bucket, access-point and identity policies as well as Block Public Access settings. For collaboration tools, revoke unintended links and guest access. Rotate any exposed secrets and assess copied or cached data.
Test anonymous denial and intended authenticated access with non-sensitive test objects. Check for alternate links and policies; public-access blocking does not revoke every authorized principal.
Use private defaults, least privilege and alerts for sharing changes. Escalate sensitive data exposure to the breach process even when no downloads are recorded.

Check each independent sharing route. Closing a public bucket policy may leave an overly broad authenticated role; revoking a document link may leave a guest account or external group. Separate intentionally public website assets from confidential material and test both after tightening controls. If access logs were not enabled during exposure, document the blind period rather than retrospectively claiming no one accessed the data. Public-access repair resolves the configuration issue; the data owner still needs an exposure assessment.

Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html
